summary: Lunar Holocron is a free, offline web application that shows, for 55 lunar landing sites and any date from 2026 to 2030, where the Sun and the Earth stand relative to the real terrain horizon. Near the lunar south pole, a ridge of a few hundred metres can decide whether a lander has sunlight and a direct line of sight to Earth. We combine NASA LOLA elevation models (5 m and 80 m) with NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides to compute each site's horizon and the Sun and Earth directions, then present them as an atlas, a 360-degree panorama, a 3D terrain view, a timeline and a communication-link page. It is built for mission planners, teachers and the public, and it states its limits openly on screen.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Near the lunar south pole the Sun skims the horizon and the Earth rises and sets with the Moon's libration. A few hundred metres of crater rim can decide whether a lander has sunlight and a direct line of sight to Earth, or neither. Existing tools give numbers in tables or flat maps that are hard to read at a glance.

WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Holocron is a static web application (no server, no network access at run time) that answers one question for each site and instant: where are the Sun and the Earth compared with the real horizon? It offers an Atlas (3D globe and 2D maps with the day/night limit and 55 sites); a Site view with a 360-degree panorama of the real horizon, a 3D terrain view showing the Sun and the Earth at their computed positions, and a timeline of elevation curves and visibility bands from 7 days to the whole 2026-2030 period; a Verdict (share of time the Sun and the Earth are visible, both together, longest periods without either, month-by-month heat map); a Link page (is the Earth above the horizon now, time to next set or rise, propagation delay, windows and outages, CSV export); a Free point tool (any latitude/longitude, computed in the browser); a Compare view; and a "Sources and method" page with provenance, formulas, definitions and limits.

HOW IT WORKS

An offline Python pipeline reads NASA data once: it builds a terrain horizon mask (360 azimuths, curvature included) for each site and computes hourly Sun and Earth azimuth, elevation and angular radius for 2026-2030 from SPICE kernels. Results are exported as JSON files. The web app (three.js, plain ES modules, no build step) only reads those files, so it works offline and is hosted as static pages on GitHub Pages.

DATA COVERAGE, STATED HONESTLY

Of the 55 sites, 27 use real LOLA 5 m terrain, 21 use LOLA 80 m terrain, and 7 (six Apollo sites and Chandrayaan-3, outside the 80 m model's coverage) have no modelled relief: a flat horizon is used and this is said on screen. A real site is evaluated at the centre of its terrain model's extent, not at a chosen landing point. Sun and Earth directions were verified against JPL Horizons (maximum difference 9e-7 degrees in azimuth). The illumination percentages are internally consistent but have not been validated against published studies; the application says so.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mission planners can compare candidate sites for solar power and direct-to-Earth line of sight. Educators can show why polar illumination is so different from the rest of the Moon. The public can explore the sky from the ground at a future landing site.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SpiceyPy, rasterio, jsonschema, pytest, Pillow), JavaScript (three.js 0.170), HTML/CSS. Code under Apache 2.0. Independent project, not endorsed by NASA.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

The same real horizon is used everywhere (panorama, 3D scene, timeline, verdict), so one ridge can be followed from a number on the timeline to the sky it blocks. The honesty rules are part of the design: data coverage and unverified positions are shown on screen, not hidden in a document.

USE OF AI

Claude Code (Anthropic) wrote the application code, the data pipeline, the tests and the technical documentation, following task files kept in the repository. Claude (Anthropic, chat) reviewed the work, recomputed some values independently and proposed priorities. The two team members set the goals, chose what to build, ran and inspected the application, and decided what to publish. A complete line-by-line human review of the code has not been recorded. Interface texts, documentation and code comments were written with these AI tools. No AI-generated images or video are used; the demo video is a screen recording with the team lead's own voice (no AI-generated audio), edited with ffmpeg.

TEAM

Victoire Ndala Mwenze (team lead) and Lionel Kisimba Kipoka, NASA Space Apps Challenge Lubumbashi 2026.
